Issued at 205 PM CDT Wed Sep 16 2026

Per a recent hand surface analysis, the Lower Great Lakes 
reside in a broad low-level baroclinic zone along the southern 
flank of an expansive high pressure system centered over Lake 
Superior and an unusually strong (600dm!) upper-level ridge 
centered over the southeastern United States. The broad region 
of low-level confluence within the baroclinic zone is supporting
a pool of unusually high moisture content across portions of 
Iowa, Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana with surface dew points in
the upper 60s to lower 70s and PWATs of 2.1 to 2.25" (near 
record highs for the middle of September). A series of weakening
MCVs are parading within the baroclinic zone, leading to areas 
of showers stretching from the IA/MO border through northern 
Illinois and into northern Ohio. 

Tonight, an upper-level wave propagating within an elongated 
upper- level jet streak along the US/Canadian border will induce
modest low- level pressure falls in the central Great Lakes. As
a result, south to southwesterly low-level flow will increase 
across the middle Mississippi River Valley (25 to 30kt at 850mb)
facilitating a gradual increase in isentropic ascent and an 
increase in shower and thunderstorm coverage within the 
baroclinic zone. Coverage of storms should first be highest 
across central Iowa near the nose of the low- level jet before 
expanding eastward into northern Illinois toward daybreak as the
direction of the low-level jet veers westerly. Storms should 
gradually weaken in intensity and coverage through the morning 
hours as the low-level jet weakens in magnitude. 

CAM-based guidance matches such a conceptual model with a 
somewhat narrow band of storms parading within the baroclinic 
zone tonight into tomorrow morning, but will note the usual 
differences in exact storm placement owing to disparity in the 
exact location of best low-level forcing. Tend to give a bit 
more preference to model outcomes that depict a more 
southeasterly trajectory in line with conglomerating outflow, 
leading to a favored corridor more or less near or just south of
the I-80 corridor. Accordingly, will feature the highest PoPs 
(>80%) near and south of I-80 tonight through tomorrow morning. 
With at least some hint of upper-level jet forcing in the 
general vicinity to facilitate weak frontogenesis, can also 
envision additional showers and storms north of the primary 
axis near the IL/WI state line, as well. So, will hold onto 
likely PoPs as far north as Rockford and Evanston through the 
morning hours.

With the aforementioned anomalously moist environment (PWATs 
perhaps ticking upward toward 2.3 to 2.4"), rain rates beneath 
thunderstorms tonight into tomorrow morning will be solidly in 
the "torrential" category. Conceptually, would expect there to 
be a stripe or two of 12-hour rainfall amounts in the 2 to 
locally 5 inch range tonight into tomorrow morning stretching 
from central Iowa through northern Illinois. Did give serious 
consideration to hoisting a Flood Watch across the area, though 
was compelled to hold off by 30-day precipitation deficits of a 
mere 10 to 20% of normal and soil moisture values well below the
seasonal values. With that said, can certainly envision areas 
of ponding water in low-lying areas where downpours are most 
persistent as well as a typical urban flash flood threat. 

After a wet morning, current expectations are for the latter 
half of Thursday and into Friday to be dry as a surface high 
pressure system builds into the Great Lakes and shunts the low- 
level baroclinic zone southward. Friday may offer the best shot 
of seeing more than a few peeks of the sun over the next several
days. Persistent onshore flow on the southern side of the 
surface high should lead to a modest lake shadow with highs 
generally ranging from around 80 inland to the mid 70s lakeside.

Attention then turns to what will be another wet period across 
the region this weekend. Ensemble guidance remains in excellent 
agreement that the upper-level wave moving across California 
will stall by midweek as the stubborn upper-level ridge across 
the southeastern US migrates toward the central Plains. As this 
occurs, an upper-level wave (or two) originating from northern 
Mexico will propagate northward across the western US and shift 
eastward toward the Midwest by Friday. Increasing upper-level 
jet diffluence and low-level convergence along the noses of an 
intensifying low-level jets should lead to hefty regions of 
showers and storms in the Upper Mississippi River Valley to our 
north and west Friday into Saturday morning. As the parent 
Pacific wave drifts eastward and a surface high pressure system 
moves into southern Canada this the weekend, a low-level frontal
zone will shift southward across the Lower Great Lakes and 
serve as a focus for several rounds of showers and storms 
Saturday afternoon through the middle of next week. Will hence
